reasoning.Student A:
My goal is to maximize my final wealth. I know my preferences are x > y > w > z. My priorities are: w: 1, x: 2, y: 1, z: 2. Other applicants seem to favor y > x > w > z.

I have high priority at w and y. I like x better than y, but my priority is higher at y. Since many applicants favor y > x, it's likely that y will be competitive. I should rank y highly to ensure I have a good chance of matching there, given my high priority.

I like x second best and have priority 2 there. Since many applicants also like x, it might be competitive even with my second priority.

I like w third best and have the highest priority there. This is a good backup option, so I should rank it after y and x.

I like z the least and have priority 2 there. I am unlikely to match to z and I don't want to.

Therefore, I will rank y > x > w > z. This reflects my preferences while accounting for my priorities and the preferences of other applicants.
reasoning.Student B: My initial preference is x > w > z > y. My priorities are x:1, w:2, y:2, z:1. I want to maximize my chances of getting matched to a school I like and have a good priority at. Since most applicants favor y > x > w > z, school y and likely school x will be very competitive. I have priority 1 at both x and z. I should stick to my preference order since I have a high priority at both my favorite (x) and a decent choice (z). I am unlikely to get my lower choices anyway.
